title: The three big Swiss banks are now available to you
what: From this month you can buy shares of Switzerland's three big banks. The Schweizerische Bankgesellschaft of Zurich is the largest: it manages the wealth of private clients from all over the world, lends to Swiss companies and households, and trades securities. The Schweizerischer Bankverein of Basel is strong in the international securities and currency markets. The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt of Zurich, called Credit Suisse abroad, is still recovering its reputation from the Chiasso scandal of 1977, in which a branch near the Italian border ran a fraudulent scheme that cost the bank about 1.4 billion francs; since 1978 it has been partnered with the US investment bank First Boston.
why: Listing beat. The Kreditanstalt is the most adventurous of the three; the First Boston link sets the course for an investment bank that it never fully controls and that eventually sinks it. [Curator note applied 2026-10-04: "Combine this story with Bankverein and Bankgesellschaft joining the game and delete the other two."]
source: https://hls-dhs-dss.ch/de/articles/041821/ (read 2026-10-03); https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/credit-suisse-group (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse (read 2026-10-03); company profiles in data/src/profiles.ts for the Bankgesellschaft and the Bankverein

title: Swiss voters keep bank secrecy
what: On 20 May Swiss voters rejected the popular initiative 'against the abuse of bank client confidentiality and bank power' by 73% to 27%; not a single canton approved it. Turnout was about 42.5%. The big banks can go on guarding their clients' secrets as before.
why: The bank-secrecy strand: three decades later Credit Suisse pleads guilty in the US for helping Americans evade taxes.

title: Swiss shares rush to new peaks
what: After a dip in September, Swiss share indexes, including the Kreditanstalt's own index, climbed to new records in October on very heavy volume. Domestic and foreign buyers are active, registered shares of the blue chips are in strong demand, and the franc firmed further against the dollar.
why: The 1985 boom: the Kreditanstalt's best twelve months in the game (+126% from February 1985 to February 1986).
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 30 November 1985, p. 23 ('Zürcher Börse vom 25. bis zum 29. November: Im Eiltempo zu neuen Gipfeln'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1985-11-30.pdf (read 2026-10-03); data/raw/fred/DEXSZUS.csv (read 2026-10-03)

title: The Kreditanstalt moves under CS Holding
what: Early in 1989 the Kreditanstalt turned CS Holding into a publicly traded umbrella company over the bank, the investment bank CS First Boston, and other holdings such as the utility Elektrowatt. The reorganisation cost about $80 million. Holders of Kreditanstalt bearer shares are offered CS Holding shares in exchange.
why: From now on the shares in the game are CS Holding's. The structure puts a Wall Street investment bank and a Swiss bank under one roof, the model that defines and finally destroys the group.

title: CS Holding wins Bank Leu in a hostile takeover
what: CS Holding completed its takeover of Bank Leu, Switzerland's oldest bank, in the first hostile takeover in Swiss banking. CS Holding is also putting $300 million of new equity into the struggling First Boston, raising its stake to 60%.
why: Gut's acquisitive strategy at home and his costly commitment to Wall Street, both years before the rivals. [Lookahead review: 'in the same year' looked back on the whole of 1990.]

title: A bank run in Thun
what: After local media reported on its finances on 3 October, crowds of depositors rushed to the offices of the Spar- und Leihkasse Thun, a regional bank heavy in mortgages; it is the first notable bank run in Switzerland in decades. Property prices have been falling since 1989, and banks with large property loans are under strain.
why: The property crisis weakens the Volksbank, which CS Holding takes over fifteen months later.

title: The Kreditanstalt takes over the Volksbank
what: On 6 January the Kreditanstalt announced it is taking over the Schweizerische Volksbank for 2.6 billion francs. The Volksbank, the fourth-largest Swiss bank, has been weakened by write-downs on property loans and had to raise its reserves to 500 million francs last year. The Bankgesellschaft, which also bid, lost out at the last moment. Chairman Rainer Gut and the new chief executive Josef Ackermann expect large savings from 1995.
why: Gut's coup: with the Volksbank's branches CS Holding becomes the Swiss bank with the most branches and number two by size.

title: CS Holding becomes Credit Suisse Group
what: In January a far-reaching reorganisation took effect: CS Holding is renamed Credit Suisse Group and organised in four business units, and about 5,000 jobs, 15% of the workforce, are to go. Chief executive Lukas Mühlemann leads the restructuring.
why: Mühlemann's modernisation; later in 1997 he adds the insurer Winterthur, a bet on 'bancassurance' that fails.

title: Credit Suisse buys Winterthur
what: In August Credit Suisse Group agreed to merge with the Winterthur insurance group for about $9.5 billion. The combined group will have total assets of about 700 billion francs and offer banking and insurance from one hand.
why: The insurance arm drags Credit Suisse down in the bear market of 2001-2002 and is sold to AXA in 2006.

title: Out of the 'new economy', back into banks
what: In March investors began to sell technology, media and telecom shares and the Nasdaq fell from its 10 March high; the hedge fund manager Julian Robertson closed his value-oriented Tiger funds, saying he no longer understood the markets. In Zurich the broad SPI rose in March, and Credit Suisse Group shares ended the month at 331 francs, their highest in a year.
why: Credit Suisse (+25%) gained from the rotation out of technology shares; no company-specific news was found for the month.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 April 2000, p. 33 ('Die überfällige Nasdaq-Korrektur'; 'Der Schweizer Aktienmarkt vom 27. bis zum 31. März: Kreuzfahrt im dichten Nebel', weekly price table), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_2000-04-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

title: Credit Suisse buys Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette
what: In November Credit Suisse completed its purchase of the US investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette for about $12.4 billion, to be merged into Credit Suisse First Boston.
why: Bought at the top of the market; in 2021 Credit Suisse writes off 1.6 billion francs of goodwill from this deal.

title: Swissair grounded
what: On 2 October the entire Swissair fleet was grounded after UBS refused to extend its credit line. UBS and Credit Suisse bought SAirGroup's stake in Crossair, which is to take over Swissair's European flights, and federal bridge loans let flights resume on 5 October. Lukas Mühlemann, chairman of Credit Suisse, sat on the Swissair board during its troubles.
why: The banks' role in the Swissair collapse damages their standing in Switzerland; Mühlemann's double role costs him credibility.

title: Rating agencies turn negative on Credit Suisse
what: In July the credit-rating agencies put Credit Suisse Group's ratings on negative outlook. The falling stock markets are eating into the capital of its insurer Winterthur, and the group is injecting capital into Winterthur and raising hybrid capital for its insurance business.
why: 2002 is Credit Suisse's worst year before 2008: a net loss of 3.3 billion francs, Mühlemann's departure, and from January 2003 the co-chief executives Oswald Grübel and John Mack. The exact news of July is softened; the 20-F records only the rating outlooks and the Winterthur measures during 2002.
source: Credit Suisse Group Form 20-F for 2002, filed 27 March 2003, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1159510/000104746903010549/a2104752z20-f.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://www.encyclopedia.com/social-sciences-and-law/economics-business-and-labor/businesses-and-occupations/credit-suisse-group (read 2026-10-03)

title: Mack leaves; Grübel runs Credit Suisse alone
what: John Mack left Credit Suisse at the end of his three-year contract in early July; Oswald Grübel, with the bank for more than 30 years, is now sole chief executive of the group. Brady Dougan becomes head of Credit Suisse First Boston and Walter Berchtold head of the Swiss bank.
why: Grübel's turnaround brings net income of 5.6 billion francs for 2004; Dougan, the investment banker, becomes group chief executive in 2007.
source: Credit Suisse Group Form 20-F for 2004, filed 30 March 2005, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1159510/000102123105000251/b78781x20-f.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Winterthur sold to AXA
what: On 14 June Credit Suisse agreed to sell the Winterthur insurance group to the French insurer AXA. The bank wants to concentrate on private banking, investment banking and asset management as one integrated bank.
why: Undoes the 1997 bancassurance bet and leaves Credit Suisse a pure bank, just before the financial crisis.

title: Mismarked positions in the CDO business
what: Credit Suisse has found mismarks and pricing errors by a small number of traders on certain asset-backed positions in its CDO trading business. Markets for mortgage-linked securities remain in turmoil.
why: A blow to Credit Suisse's claim to have handled the credit crisis better than UBS. The 20-F places the discovery only in the first quarter; February is when the share fell 14%. [Lookahead review: dropped the material-weakness conclusion and the quarter framing, both from the later 20-F.]

title: Credit Suisse raises 10 billion francs without the state
what: On 16 October, the day the Swiss state rescued UBS, Credit Suisse announced it had raised new capital from a small group of investors, about 10 billion francs from three existing shareholders; Qatar Holding reported holding 8.9% of the shares on 22 October. Credit Suisse said it would not use the National Bank's facility for illiquid assets. The bank cancelled its share buyback.
why: Credit Suisse survives the crisis without state aid, a point of pride that later makes it harder to admit weakness. The new shares and the crash pushed the stock down 23% in October.
source: Credit Suisse Form 20-F for 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1053092/000137036809000006/a090324ar20f.htm (read 2026-10-03); Swiss National Bank, media release of 16 October 2008 (read 2026-10-03)

title: Credit Suisse earns 2 billion francs in the first quarter
what: On 23 April Credit Suisse reported net income of 2,006 million francs for the first quarter of 2009, against a loss of 2,148 million a year earlier. Private Banking attracted 11.4 billion francs of new money. Chief executive Brady Dougan said the bank was reaping the rewards of its early action to cut risk.
why: Credit Suisse looks like the crisis winner among Swiss banks (+26% again in April); 2009 net income reaches 6.7 billion francs.

title: The National Bank caps the franc
what: On 6 September the Swiss National Bank set a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro and promised to buy foreign currency in unlimited amounts to defend it. The franc, which had soared during the euro crisis, fell about 11% against the dollar in September.
why: For dollar investors the weaker franc adds to the fall in Swiss bank shares (Credit Suisse -9%).

title: Credit Suisse pleads guilty in the US
what: On 19-20 May Credit Suisse pleaded guilty in the United States to conspiring to help American clients evade taxes, and agreed to pay about $2.6 billion in fines and restitution.
why: The tax strand reaches Credit Suisse five years after UBS; the plea and the management's survival damage its reputation.

title: Thiam's new strategy and 6 billion francs of new capital
what: On 21 October chief executive Tidjane Thiam, in office since July, announced a new strategy: Credit Suisse wants to be a leading private bank and wealth manager with investment banking capabilities, organised in regional divisions. He also announced a capital increase of about 6 billion francs through a private placement and a rights offering, and six new members of the executive board.
why: The first of several restructurings and capital raises; the rights issue is not adjusted in the price series.

title: A 5.8-billion-franc quarterly loss
what: On 4 February Credit Suisse reported a net loss of 5,828 million francs for the fourth quarter of 2015, including a goodwill write-off of 3,797 million, mostly in its trading business; the full-year 2015 loss was 2,944 million francs.
why: Thiam's first full results reveal how little the old investment bank was worth (-25% in the month).
source: Credit Suisse Earnings Release 4Q15 (Form 6-K of 4 February 2016), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1053092/000137036816000102/a160204g4q-ex99_1.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: The end of bank secrecy for foreign clients
what: From 2017 Switzerland applies the international standard for the automatic exchange of information on bank accounts: Swiss banks collect data on accounts of foreign residents, which will be sent to their home tax authorities from 2018. For depositors who do not live in Switzerland, bank secrecy is effectively over.
why: Closes the bank-secrecy strand that began with the 1984 vote.

title: Thiam resigns over the spying affair
what: In the final months of 2019 it emerged that Credit Suisse had had former executives, among them the wealth manager Iqbal Khan, followed by private detectives; the chief operating officer Pierre-Olivier Bouée left. On 7 February Tidjane Thiam announced his resignation as chief executive. Thomas Gottstein, head of the Swiss bank, succeeds him on 14 February. At the end of the month markets began to fall as the coronavirus spread.
why: The observation affair shows a culture problem at the top; from here the decline accelerates.

title: Covid crash
what: Markets crashed as the coronavirus spread: the S&P 500 fell 7.6% on 9 March, 9.5% on 12 March and about 12% on 16 March, after the Federal Reserve had cut its rate to zero. On 20 March the Swiss government announced an economic aid programme.
why: Credit Suisse lost 28% in the month, twice as much as UBS.

title: Vaccine hopes lift the banks
what: Pfizer and BioNTech reported in November that their coronavirus vaccine had met its efficacy goals in the final trial, with a potential efficacy of more than 90%. Share markets rallied; the S&P 500 gained about 11% in November.
why: A market beat (+33% for Credit Suisse, its best month after 1998).

title: Greensill and Archegos in one month
what: On 1 March Credit Suisse froze four supply-chain finance funds with about $10 billion of assets, which it ran with Greensill Capital; on 4 March it decided to liquidate them, and Greensill filed for insolvency on 8 March. At the end of the month the US family office Archegos Capital failed to meet margin calls and its lending banks, Credit Suisse among them, began selling the positions they held for it.
why: The double blow that starts the endgame: the funds were sold to wealthy clients, the core franchise, and Archegos shows a failure of risk control in the investment bank (-27% in the month).

title: A 4.4-billion-franc hit from Archegos
what: Credit Suisse booked a provision for credit losses of 4,430 million francs for the first quarter on the Archegos default. The chief risk officer Lara Warner left on 6 April and the head of the investment bank, Brian Chin, stepped down; the board withdrew its pay proposal for the executive board and revised its dividend proposal. On 22 April the bank placed mandatory convertible notes of about 1.76 billion francs to rebuild capital. António Horta-Osório was elected chairman on 30 April.
why: Archegos costs 4.8 billion francs in total; the external report of July finds failures of risk management in the prime-services business.

title: Körner's rescue plan: 4 billion francs and 9,000 jobs
what: After rumours about its health spread on social media early in the month, Credit Suisse announced on 27 October a fourth consecutive quarterly loss and a new plan: a capital increase of 4 billion francs, with the Saudi National Bank investing up to 1.5 billion for a stake of up to 9.9%; about 9,000 jobs cut by 2025; and a separate investment bank, CS First Boston, to be built up under Michael Klein. The shares opened 14% lower at 4.10 francs.
why: The last strategy. The rumours triggered withdrawals of 110 billion francs in the fourth quarter; the rights issue that follows is not adjusted in the price series and is part of November's -20%.

title: 7.3 billion francs lost, 110 billion withdrawn
what: On 9 February Credit Suisse reported a net loss of 7.3 billion francs for 2022, its worst since 2008, and net outflows of 110.5 billion francs of client money in the fourth quarter after rumours about its stability.
why: The outflows show that clients, not markets, are deciding the bank's fate.

title: Forced into the arms of UBS
what: On 14 March Credit Suisse published its 2022 annual report, saying it had found material weaknesses in its financial-reporting controls. On 15 March the chairman of its largest shareholder, the Saudi National Bank, said it would 'absolutely not' invest more; the shares fell about a quarter that day. The Swiss National Bank lent 50 billion francs on 16 March. On Sunday 19 March the government announced that UBS takes over Credit Suisse for 3 billion francs, one UBS share for 22.48 Credit Suisse shares, under emergency law without a shareholder vote; 16 billion francs of AT1 bonds are written off.
why: The end of Credit Suisse as an independent bank (-71% in March). The parliamentary inquiry later blames mismanagement at the bank.

title: Credit Suisse disappears into UBS
what: On 12 June UBS completed the takeover; Credit Suisse Group became a subsidiary of UBS and its shares were exchanged at one UBS share for 22.48 Credit Suisse shares. The shares had fallen to about 1.55 francs in March, against more than 90 francs in 2007.
why: Exit beat: holders now own UBS. Over 41 years in the game the share lost 89% in dollars, and 99% from its 2007 peak.
